title: Efficient Morphology-Control Co-Design via Stackelberg Proximal Policy Optimization
claim: Our method evolves a bare initial design into a complex, task-capable form, while the baseline stays simple and ineffective.
layout: 2 rows, left-to-right training timeline, final-task render panels at right
description: The figure has two horizontal rows of orange, stick-like robot morphologies. A grey arrow labeled "Training Process" runs across the top, with ticks at 0%, 5%, 20%, 60% and 100%. The top row is "Stackelberg PPO (ours)". It starts as a small body with three stubby limbs and grows into a large, multi-limbed structure with long arm-like and leg-like branches. The bottom row is "PPO". It starts from the same bare body and ends with a simpler, sparser set of limbs. Two rendered scenes sit at the far right, one per row. Each shows the final robot on a purple checkerboard floor next to a large red cube. In the top scene the robot pushes the cube with its arms. In the bottom scene the robot is small and positioned in front of the cube. The eye goes first to the top row's growth sequence, then to the red cubes.
caption: Showcasing how our Stackelberg PPO can autonomously design task-specific robots for the “Pusher” task, starting with a bare-bones structure and ultimately evolving into a sophisticated design with arm-like structures for pushing boxes and leg-like limbs for movement. This highlights the method’s ability to create adaptive and complex designs. In comparison, the traditional PPO method generates simpler structures that can’t support more complex behaviors. For more examples of evolved designs and animations, as well as open-source code, visit: https://yanningdai.github.io/stackelberg-ppo-co-design.
abstract: Morphology-control co-design concerns the coupled optimization of an agent's body structure and control policy. This problem exhibits a bi-level structure, where the control dynamically adapts to the morphology to maximize performance. Existing methods typically neglect the control's adaptation dynamics by adopting a single-level formulation that treats the control policy as fixed when optimizing morphology. This can lead to inefficient optimization, as morphology updates may be misaligned with control adaptation. In this paper, we revisit the co-design problem from a game-theoretic perspective, modeling the intrinsic coupling between morphology and control as a novel variant of a Stackelberg game. We propose Stackelberg Proximal Policy Optimization (Stackelberg PPO), which explicitly incorporates the control's adaptation dynamics into morphology optimization. By modeling this intrinsic coupling, our method aligns morphology updates with control adaptation, thereby stabilizing training and improving learning efficiency. Experiments across diverse co-design tasks demonstrate that Stackelberg PPO outperforms standard PPO in both stability and final performance, opening the way for dramatically more efficient robotics designs.
